children.text: We’re introduced to Pastor Paul’s main argument, that churches who shun queer members are theologically insecure, and the counter argument, no churches have to stay pure. Pastor Paul’s ethos is established by his clerical clothing, along with what looks like some sort of pride pin; this clothing choice also separates the two characters he is playing, the progressive pastor and the conservative christian. He’s positioned in front of a bookshelf that, while in the frame of the video, is completely filled with books which lets the viewer know he is well read, or at least pushing the image of someone who reads a lot.

‘Jesus tells us to love our enemies’ he supports this statement with logos showing the scriptures he's pulling from on the screen (Matthew 5:44, and Luke 6:35), and the use of cited sources shows his reliability, and genuine knowledge of the bible. The fact he pulls two different scriptures, written by different people adds credence to his argument, that shunning those deemed impure by some churches is a teaching directly against the bible. It also invites the viewer to look up the scriptures for themselves to come to their own conclusions, and see the context in which the scripture is pulled from.

Here he is actively using scripture to defend the LGBTQIA community (and anyone else the opposition believes is impure) which appeals to the viewers compassion and sense of justice, from the opposite perspective who calls them sinners and implying that they aren't welcome at church. The fact he has the opposing argument to call those he disapproves of sinners and harmful to the purity of the church is an argument in pathos, but instead of pushing his argument it's pushing for the viewer to see the opposition in a negative light. This pushing between two arguments is allowed by the style of content he posts.

His defense of the LGBT+ community also hints at his audience, while his audience is not just queer people, his defense and support of them show that they are welcome on his page. The set up of the debate also alludes to the audience he is aiming towards, people who might have the same views as his opponent. In fact I would say he is trying to reach the people who believe in these more conservative christians because of how focused he is on deconstructing their ideas and the unintended audience is queer people and those that hold more progressive views of Christianity.

Here Pastor Paul argues that our modern society is different from the society that wrote these scriptures and that taking a general idea from what the bible teaches and applying it to our modern conflicts. In this instance he is using a scripture that says supporting our sisters and brothers in the light will stop them from stumbling (which seems to be saying that loving our fellow christians will stop them from falling into sin), and using it to support queer people. This is using a mix of judicial and epideictic rhetoric, the beliefs that Jesus thought in the past are not aligning with the church’s current teachings, and that using the bible as a strict set of rules isn’t the only way to apply the bible to our current society.

For a little bit of context, the opposing perspective argues against the loving sinners asking if he should love a murderer, as they are also sinners. This is countered by Pastor Paul when he argues that Jesus didn't condemn the people that murdered him while he is actively being crucified, when he could have called down the armies of angels. He argues that churches who preach that they should shun sinners are teaching an anti-christian theology. The delivery of this statement stands out as he breaks his calm demeanor, he speaks passionately about Jesus and his love.

He finishes his argument in agreement with the opposing argument that being a christian is hard, because you have to love sinners to help guide them to salvation which can be a messy situation. The opposing perspective has also come to a reluctant agreement that his church shouldn't demonize queer people. This contributes to the persona he has built up, a loving pastor who welcomes all, as he not only supports those that have been wronged by christians, but also supports those who are recovering from the extremes of christianity and trying to deradicalize their harmful views.

* In the caption of the video, he talks about how there are caveats for casting out members of a church, like those that threaten to harm others. However, he also mentions that often those he sees being cast out are just ‘theologically inconvenient’, which is sinful. He quotes another scripture, this one about bearing one another's burdens. The addition of a cation is an affordance given by the platform, and it allows him to expand his argument. This expansion includes more quoting of scripture, showing once again that he knows the Bible. He also admits that there are cases where churches should cast people out. The citing of those who threaten others as the example of when to cast someone out is pathos. He also plays into the algorithm in the caption as he tags his posts with ‘progressive pastor’ which pushes his content to a more religious and progressive audience who would enjoy his arguments.
